assignment.title: Remainder & Factor Theorems — Honors
assignment.essentialQuestion: What relationships exist between the factors of polynomial expressions and the zeros of their associated polynomial functions?
assignment.teacherNotes: Honors version of Bluebonnet Algebra II — Polynomials, Lesson 2 (Factoring Using the Remainder, Factor, and Rational Zero Theorems), TEKS A2.7D (A2.7C, A2.7E). Beyond the regular lesson: why the Remainder Theorem works, zeros and remainders read from tables, leading coefficients other than 1, long division by 2x − 1 and by quadratics, parameters fixed by remainders (one and two unknowns), irrational zeros, building a polynomial from its zeros, a volume model, and factor questions answered without dividing. Synthetic and long division happen in the Polynomial Workshop; rational-zero lists are sets and may use ±. Practice includes two audited SAT items (MathMaster CCMR bank). Warm-Up and DOL are generated per student and back Recovery.

Split the middle term with those two numbers and factor by grouping.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For {{a}}x² {{b|xterm}} {{c|signed}}, the product a · c is…

solutionReview.headline: Product ac, sum b, split, group.
reasoning: a · c = {{ac}}; {{m1}} and {{m2}} have product {{ac}} and sum {{b}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Looking for two numbers whose product is c: in the ac method their product is a · c.

hints: Substitute {{r}} for x and set the result equal to {{v}}.

questions.prompt: Divide $P(x) = 2x^4 - 7x^3 + 5x - 10$ by $x - 3$ with synthetic division — a missing power needs a 0. Then read the bottom row: what is the quotient, and what is $P(3)$?

steps.title: Remainder Theorem
steps.instruction: When P(x) is divided by x − r, the remainder is P(r): P(x) = (x − r)·Q(x) + P(r).

steps.title: Synthetic division
steps.instruction: Box r; write every coefficient from the highest power down, with a 0 for each missing power; bring down, multiply by r, add, repeat.

steps.title: Reading the bottom row
steps.instruction: The last entry is the remainder P(r); the others are the quotient’s coefficients, one degree lower.

hints: Five coefficients for a fourth-degree polynomial: one of them is 0.
The last number in the bottom row is the remainder, which equals P(3).

solutionReview.commonError: Leaving out the 0 for the missing x² term: every coefficient after it shifts, and the remainder comes out wrong.

questions.prompt: Why the Remainder Theorem works. Dividing $P(x)$ by $x - r$ gives $P(x) = (x - r)Q(x) + R$, where the remainder $R$ is a number. Use that equation to reason.

responses.label: Substitute x = r. Why does P(r) = R?
options: (r − r)Q(r) = 0 · Q(r) = 0, so only R is left
r is always a factor of R
responses.answer: (r − r)Q(r) = 0 · Q(r) = 0, so only R is left

responses.label: If P(5) = 0, which must be true?
options: x − 5 is a factor of P(x)
x + 5 is a factor of P(x)
5 is the constant term of P(x)
P(x) has no other real zeros
responses.answer: x − 5 is a factor of P(x)

responses.label: Without dividing: the remainder when x³ − 4x² + 6 is divided by x − 3 is
Ana says x + 2 is a factor of P(x) because P(2) = 0. What is her error?
options: P(2) = 0 makes x − 2 a factor; x + 2 is a factor when P(−2) = 0
There is no error: P(2) = 0 means x + 2 is a factor
responses.answer: P(2) = 0 makes x − 2 a factor; x + 2 is a factor when P(−2) = 0

hints: Replace every x in P(x) = (x − r)Q(x) + R with r.
x − r is a factor exactly when the remainder is 0.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is (r − r) · Q(r)?

solutionReview.headline: Substitute r into the division equation.
reasoning: P(5) = 0 means the remainder of P(x) ÷ (x − 5) is 0, so x − 5 is a factor.
x + 2 = x − (−2) is a factor exactly when P(−2) = 0; P(2) = 0 makes x − 2 a factor.
solutionReview.answerSummary: P(r) = R; x − 5 is a factor; remainder −3; Ana confused x − 2 with x + 2
solutionReview.commonError: Mixing up the sign: P(2) = 0 makes x − 2 a factor, not x + 2.

questions.prompt: Read a table with the Factor and Remainder Theorems. The table shows values of a cubic $P(x)$ with leading coefficient 1.

responses.label: Zeros of P, as a set
The remainder when P(x) is divided by x − 4
Is x + 1 a factor of P(x)?
options: It cannot be decided from the table

hints: A zero is an input where P(x) = 0.
By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder of P(x) ÷ (x − r) is P(r).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If P(1) = 0, which binomial is a factor of P(x)?

solutionReview.headline: Zeros in the table give the factors; table values give remainders.
reasoning: P(x) = 0 at x = −2, 1 and 3, so the zeros are −2, 1 and 3.
Each zero c gives a factor x − c, and the leading coefficient is 1: P(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3). Check: P(0) = (2)(−1)(−3) = 6, as in the table.
The remainder of P(x) ÷ (x − 4) is P(4) = 18.
P(−1) = 8 ≠ 0, so x + 1 is not a factor.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing x + c for a zero c: a zero at x = c gives the factor x − c.

questions.prompt: The Rational Zero Theorem with a leading coefficient other than 1. Factor $P(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 11x + 6$ completely and find its zeros.

responses.label: Possible rational zeros p/q, as a set

steps.title: Rational Zero Theorem
steps.instruction: If P(x) has integer coefficients, every rational zero is p/q, where p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient.

steps.title: Factoring a cubic
steps.instruction: List the candidates, test them until P(r) = 0, divide by x − r, then factor the quadratic quotient (the ac method when its leading coefficient is not 1).

hints: p divides 6 and q divides 2.
Test the integer candidates first; the bottom row of the synthetic division gives the quotient.
Factor the quadratic quotient with the ac method.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In the Rational Zero Theorem, q is a factor of…

solutionReview.headline: Candidates, a zero, the quotient, then the ac method.
reasoning: p is ±1, ±2, ±3 or ±6 and q is ±1 or ±2, so the candidates are ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6, ±1/2 and ±3/2.
P(3) = 54 − 27 − 33 + 6 = 0, so x − 3 is a factor; synthetic division by 3 leaves 2x² + 3x − 2.
The zeros are 3, 1/2 and −2 — one is a fraction, which is why the candidate list includes p/q.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving out the fractions ±1/2 and ±3/2: the leading coefficient 2 makes them candidates.

questions.prompt: Synthetic division needs a divisor of the form $x - r$. For $2x - 1$, use long division: divide $6x^3 + 7x^2 - x - 2$ by $2x - 1$.

steps.title: Long division
steps.instruction: Divide the leading terms, multiply the whole divisor by that quotient term, subtract, and bring down the next term. Stop when the remainder has a lower degree than the divisor.

hints: Divide the leading terms first: 6x³ ÷ 2x.
Multiply that quotient term by 2x − 1, subtract, bring down the next term, and repeat.

solutionReview.commonError: Subtracting only the first term at each step: subtract the whole product of the new quotient term and 2x − 1.

questions.prompt: Long division gave $6x^3 + 7x^2 - x - 2 = (2x - 1)(3x^2 + 5x + 2)$. Synthetic division by $x - \tfrac{1}{2}$ gives the bottom row $6,\ 10,\ 4 \mid 0$ instead. Connect the two results, then factor completely.

responses.label: Why is the synthetic-division quotient 6x² + 10x + 4 twice the long-division quotient?
options: 2x − 1 = 2(x − 1/2), so dividing by x − 1/2 leaves the factor 2 inside the quotient
Synthetic division always doubles the quotient
One of the two divisions is wrong
responses.answer: 2x − 1 = 2(x − 1/2), so dividing by x − 1/2 leaves the factor 2 inside the quotient

hints: Multiply out 2(x − 1/2).
Factor 3x² + 5x + 2 with the ac method: a · c = 6.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. 2(x − 1/2) equals…

solutionReview.headline: The two divisions differ by the factor 2 in the divisor.
solutionReview.commonError: Taking 6x² + 10x + 4 as the quotient for 2x − 1: dividing by x − 1/2 leaves an extra factor of 2 in it.

questions.prompt: Divide $x^4 + 2x^3 - 3x^2 + 5x - 1$ by $x^2 + x - 1$. With a quadratic divisor the remainder can be linear: stop when its degree is less than 2.
hints: The first quotient term is x⁴ ÷ x².
The remainder has degree less than 2, so it can have an x-term.

solutionReview.commonError: Stopping too early or too late: keep dividing until the remainder’s degree is less than 2, the degree of the divisor.

questions.prompt: A remainder fixes a parameter. When $P(x) = x^3 + kx^2 - 4x + 3$ is divided by $x - 2$, the remainder is $15$. Find $k$, then test another factor.

responses.label: So is x + 1 a factor of P(x)?
options: Yes — −1 is a possible rational zero
It cannot be decided without dividing

hints: The remainder of P(x) ÷ (x − 2) is P(2).
Set P(2) = 15 and solve the linear equation for k.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The remainder when P(x) is divided by x − 2 equals…

solutionReview.headline: The Remainder Theorem turns the remainder into an equation.
reasoning: P(x) = x³ + 3x² − 4x + 3 and P(−1) = −1 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 9 ≠ 0, so x + 1 is not a factor.
solutionReview.commonError: Setting P(2) = 0: the remainder is 15, so P(2) = 15.

questions.prompt: Two conditions, two unknowns. $P(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 6$ has a factor $x - 1$, and leaves remainder $-12$ when divided by $x + 2$. Find $a$ and $b$, then factor $P(x)$.

responses.label: P(x) completely factored over the integers
Number of real zeros of P

hints: Write one equation from the factor x − 1 and one from the remainder −12.
Add the two equations to eliminate b.
Is the discriminant of the quadratic factor positive, zero, or negative?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If P(x) leaves remainder −12 when divided by x + 2, then…

solutionReview.headline: Each condition is one equation.
reasoning: P(x) = x³ + 2x² + 3x − 6 = (x − 1)(x² + 3x + 6). The quadratic has discriminant 9 − 24 < 0, so P has exactly one real zero, x = 1.
solutionReview.commonError: Setting P(−2) = 0 for the second condition: a remainder of −12 means P(−2) = −12.

questions.prompt: Irrational zeros. Find every zero of $P(x) = x^4 - x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x + 4$: two are rational and two are not.

responses.label: Possible rational zeros, as a set
After dividing by x − 1, the depressed cubic is
After dividing that cubic by x + 2, the quadratic factor is

hints: Test the candidates with synthetic division; x = 1 works first.
Keep a 0 for any missing power when you divide again.
The quadratic factor does not factor over the integers: use the quadratic formula.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The quadratic formula gives the zeros of ax² + bx + c as…

solutionReview.headline: Divide out the rational zeros, then use the quadratic formula.
reasoning: The candidates are ±1, ±2 and ±4. P(1) = 1 − 1 − 6 + 2 + 4 = 0, and dividing by x − 1 leaves x³ − 6x − 4.
For the cubic, x = −2 works: dividing by x + 2 leaves x² − 2x − 2.

questions.prompt: Build the polynomial. Write the cubic function with zeros $-2$, $1$ and $4$ whose graph passes through $(0, 16)$.
hints: Each zero c gives a factor x − c, and a leading coefficient a multiplies the product.
Substitute the point (0, 16) to find a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Every cubic with zeros −2, 1 and 4 has the form…

solutionReview.headline: Zeros give the factors; one point gives the leading coefficient.
solutionReview.commonError: Using x − 2 for the zero −2: a zero c gives the factor x − c, so −2 gives x + 2.

questions.prompt: Use synthetic division to divide $P(x) = {{a|coef}}x^4 {{b|signed}}x^3 {{c|xterm}} {{d|signed}}$ by $x {{nr|signed}}$. Give the quotient and $P({{r}})$.
hints: A 0 holds the place of the missing x² term.

solutionReview.commonError: Boxing the wrong sign: dividing by x − r uses r, so x + 2 uses −2 and x − 3 uses 3.

questions.prompt: Find $k$ so that $x {{nr|signed}}$ is a factor of $P(x) = x^3 {{b|signed}}x^2 + kx {{d|signed}}$.
hints: A factor x − r means P(r) = 0.
Substitute x = {{r}}, set the result equal to 0, and solve for k.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x {{nr|signed}} is a factor of P(x) exactly when…

solutionReview.headline: The Factor Theorem gives one equation in k.
reasoning: x {{nr|signed}} is a factor exactly when P({{r}}) = 0.
solutionReview.commonError: Substituting x = {{nr}}: the factor x {{nr|signed}} is 0 at x = {{r}}.

questions.prompt: $x {{nr|signed}}$ is a factor of $P(x) = {{A}}x^3 {{B|signed}}x^2 {{C|xterm}} {{D|signed}}$. Factor $P(x)$ completely.
hints: Divide by x {{nr|signed}} with synthetic division.
The quotient is a quadratic with leading coefficient {{a}}: factor it with the ac method.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Dividing by x {{nr|signed}} with synthetic division, the number in the box is…

solutionReview.headline: Divide by the factor you know, then use the ac method.
reasoning: Synthetic division by {{r}} leaves the quotient {{a}}x² {{qb|xterm}} {{qc|signed}}, with remainder 0.

questions.prompt: Divide $2x^4 - x^3 - 2x - 2$ by $x^2 - x + 2$. There is no $x^2$ term in the dividend.
hints: Write the dividend with a 0 for the missing x² term.
Stop when the remainder has a lower degree than the divisor.

solutionReview.commonError: Leaving out the 0x² placeholder in the dividend: the subtraction then lines up the wrong powers.

questions.prompt: Factor $P(x) = 2x^4 + x^3 - 8x^2 - x + 6$ completely and list its zeros.

responses.label: Possible rational zeros, as a set

hints: p divides 6 and q divides 2.
Find one zero, divide, and repeat on the cubic that is left.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. After you find two zeros of a quartic and divide twice, what is left?

solutionReview.headline: Find a zero, divide, repeat, then factor the quadratic.
reasoning: For the cubic, x = −1 works: dividing by x + 1 leaves 2x² + x − 6 = (2x − 3)(x + 2).
solutionReview.commonError: Testing only integer candidates: with leading coefficient 2, ±1/2 and ±3/2 are candidates too.

questions.prompt: $P(x) = 2x^3 + ax^2 + bx + 6$ has $P(1) = 0$ and $P(-1) = 10$. Find $a$ and $b$, then factor $P(x)$ completely.
hints: Write one equation from P(1) = 0 and one from P(−1) = 10.
Add the two equations to find a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. P(1) = 0 tells you that…
options: x − 1 is a factor of P(x)
x + 1 is a factor of P(x)
scaffold.correct: x − 1 is a factor of P(x)

solutionReview.headline: Two conditions, two equations; then factor.
solutionReview.commonError: Mixing up signs in P(−1): (−1)³ = −1 and (−1)² = 1, so P(−1) = −2 + a − b + 6.

questions.prompt: The table shows values of a quartic $P(x)$ with leading coefficient 1. Three of its zeros appear in the table; the fourth does not. Use $P(0)$ to find it.

responses.label: The three zeros in the table, as a set

hints: Write P(x) = (x + 2)(x + 1)(x − 1)(x − c) and substitute x = 0.
Set your expression for P(0) equal to the table value at x = 0.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. At x = 0, the factor x − c equals…

solutionReview.headline: Three zeros from the table, the fourth from P(0).
reasoning: P(x) = 0 at x = −2, −1 and 1, so with leading coefficient 1, P(x) = (x + 2)(x + 1)(x − 1)(x − c).
P(0) = (2)(1)(−1)(−c) = 2c, and the table gives P(0) = 10, so c = 5.
solutionReview.commonError: Treating P(0) = 10 as a zero: P(0) is the product (2)(1)(−1)(−c), and that fixes c.

solutionReview.headline: The Factor Theorem gives one equation in k.
solutionReview.commonError: Substituting x = −{{a}}: the factor x − {{a}} is 0 at x = {{a}}.

questions.prompt: Find every zero of $P(x) = x^4 - 5x^3 + 3x^2 + 7x - 2$. Two are rational and two are irrational.

responses.label: The rational zeros, as a set
The quadratic factor left after dividing out both

hints: The candidates are ±1 and ±2. Test them with synthetic division.
Use the quadratic formula on the quadratic factor.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Irrational zeros of a polynomial with integer coefficients come in pairs of the form…

solutionReview.headline: Divide out the rational zeros, then use the quadratic formula.
reasoning: P(2) = 16 − 40 + 12 + 14 − 2 = 0, and dividing by x − 2 leaves x³ − 3x² − 3x + 1, which has the zero −1.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at the rational zeros: the quadratic left after dividing still has two irrational zeros.

questions.prompt: Divide $P(x) = {{A}}x^3 {{B|signed}}x^2 {{C|xterm}} {{D|signed}}$ by $2x - 1$ with long division.
hints: Divide the leading terms, multiply the divisor by that term, subtract, and bring down the next term.

solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting to change both signs when you subtract the product of the new quotient term and 2x − 1.

questions.prompt: Modeling. A box has volume $V(x) = x^3 + 4x^2 + x - 6$ cubic inches, and each dimension is a linear expression in $x$. (a) Factor $V(x)$ to find the dimensions. (b) For which $x$ is the volume 60 cubic inches? Solve $x^3 + 4x^2 + x - 66 = 0$ with the Rational Zero Theorem.

responses.label: The shortest dimension at that x (inches)
Why is that the only x that works?
options: Dividing x³ + 4x² + x − 66 by x − 3 leaves x² + 7x + 22, which has no real zeros
A cubic always has exactly one real zero
The other candidates are all negative
Volume formulas have one solution by definition
responses.answer: Dividing x³ + 4x² + x − 66 by x − 3 leaves x² + 7x + 22, which has no real zeros

hints: For (a), the candidates are the factors of the constant term, with both signs.
For (b), the candidates are the factors of 66; check that every dimension is positive.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To solve V(x) = 60, you first rewrite it as…

solutionReview.headline: Factor the model, then solve with the same tools.
reasoning: V(1) = 1 + 4 + 1 − 6 = 0, so x − 1 is a factor; dividing leaves x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3). V(x) = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x + 3).
At x = 3 the dimensions are 2, 5 and 6 inches (volume 60).
Dividing by x − 3 leaves x² + 7x + 22, whose discriminant 49 − 88 is negative, so x = 3 is the only real solution.
solutionReview.commonError: Answering x = 1 from the factor x − 1: that makes the volume 0; a volume of 60 needs x³ + 4x² + x − 66 = 0.

solutionReview.headline: Division undone is multiplication.
reasoning: The constant term of the product is {{p}} · {{r}} = {{k}}, so k = {{k}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding {{p}} and {{r}}: the constant term of a product is the product of the constant terms.

questions.prompt: No dividing allowed. Use the Factor and Remainder Theorems to decide each.

responses.label: Is x − 1 a factor of x⁹⁹ − 1?
options: It cannot be decided without dividing

responses.label: Is x + 1 a factor of x⁹⁹ + 1?
options: No — a sum of two terms never has a factor
It cannot be decided without dividing

responses.label: The remainder when x¹⁰⁰ + 1 is divided by x + 1
So is x + 1 a factor of x¹⁰⁰ + 1?
options: Yes — every binomial is a factor of x¹⁰⁰ + 1
It cannot be decided without dividing

hints: x − r is a factor exactly when P(r) = 0, and the remainder of P(x) ÷ (x − r) is P(r).
An odd power of −1 is −1; an even power of −1 is 1.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (−1)⁹⁹ equals…

solutionReview.headline: Evaluate instead of dividing.
reasoning: P(1) = 1⁹⁹ − 1 = 0, so x − 1 is a factor of x⁹⁹ − 1.
(−1)⁹⁹ + 1 = −1 + 1 = 0, so x + 1 is a factor of x⁹⁹ + 1.
(−1)¹⁰⁰ + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2, so the remainder is 2 and x + 1 is not a factor of x¹⁰⁰ + 1.
solutionReview.commonError: Treating an even power like an odd one: (−1)¹⁰⁰ = 1, so x¹⁰⁰ + 1 leaves the remainder 2.
